quotes.note: A general aphorism with no story-specific narrator evidence.
A joke presented entirely as character speech; its first-person pronouns belong to speakers within the joke.
The clipped fragment omits its grammatical subject; 'his' alone cannot distinguish third-person narration from a first-person narrator describing someone else.
The fragment and trailing comma obscure whether 'my' is dialogue, direct thought, or base narration.
This may be free-indirect base narration, but one named third-person character and her mental state do not independently establish narrator participation.

web_evidence.title: Easy Prey — Preview
web_evidence.note: The authorized three-chapter preview sustains nonparticipating third-person narration across scenes focalized through the unnamed killer, Alie'e Maison, Lucas Davenport, and others; first-person forms occur locally in speech, thought, and an email.

web_evidence.title: Easy Prey Analysis
web_evidence.note: The book-level style analysis explicitly identifies the narrative as primarily third-person limited through Davenport, with access to his thoughts and perceptions.

person_note: The controlling narrator is nonparticipating and third person. The authorized opening sustains that position across three chapters and several focal characters, while the whole-book eNotes analysis explicitly corroborates third-person limited narration. The Goodreads material is sparse: its dialogue and aphorism are non-base, and the two clipped fragments cannot safely identify a narrator. The isolated 'my' therefore does not contradict the third-person structure. Confidence is medium because the strongest primary prose evidence covers only the opening and the whole-book corroboration is Tier C rather than a structural Tier A/B source.
